body:
Hey @TobiasAhnoff there is an interesting recent article about an active device code flow phishing attack that is quite successful.

https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2025/02/russian-spies-use-device-code-phishing-to-hijack-microsoft-accounts/

Is there anything we will pull out of this for ASVS? If not you can close out this issue.

Thank you @TobiasAhnoff !!!

comments.body:
This attack is [described](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security#name-user-transferred-session-dat) (I think) in the "Cross-Device Flows: Security Best Current Practice" draft.

Mitigations are discussed in [section 6](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security#name-mitigating-against-cross-de). It might be useful to have a dedicated section about this topic. (in V2.7?)

"V5.7 Consent Management" is related to this. By ensuring the user consent this type of attack can be somewhat mitigated (but people don't read consent screens …). However, this topic/issue is more general that OAuth flows and it would be better if the requirements were in another chapter.

"V2.7 Out-of-Band authentication mechanisms" is what is the more appropriate, I think. however:

* This is not only for authentication but for delegated authorization as well. I think, this could still fit in this section.
* V2.7 seems to be currently about flows where a code is sent to the user to a third party device channel and must then be entered in the application (in the session). The alternative scenario where the user uses another application (eg. a mobile application) to authorize the access (and where the consumption device is not the same as the authorization device) is not really covered in the current requirements too much, I think.

I think this looks like a great candidate for a new requirement for 2.7.9.

Since we are getting close to the end of 5.0, I just want to make sure @elarlang and @tghosth are on board before we go to PR, but based on the suggestions from @TobiasAhnoff and @randomstuff I think we are pretty close.

> "device code phising"

Device code phishing seems to refer about OAUth [Device Code Grant](https://oauth.net/2/device-flow/) more specifically. Maybe a more general "cross-device fishing attack" could be used?

For reference, [draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security) talks about:

* Cross-Device *Consent* Phishing (CDCP) → fishing to get a delegated access (eg. access token);
* Cross-Device *Session* Phishing (CDSP)  → fishing to get a session.

I propose some small changes:

> Verify that if cross-device flows are used for authentication or delegating authorization, mitigations are in place to limit the risk of cross-device fishing. This may for example includes unique binding code or proximity checks (geolocation, network, NFC, BLE, etc).

Changes:

* cross-device solutions → cross-device flows
* device code phising → cross-device fishing
* unique QR codes → unique binding code
* move the proximity checks at the end (because I feel they are less widely applicable)
* add NFC and BLE as a proximity check
A related topic is MFA fatigue attack / MFA bombing / MFA spamming. Would it be useful to explicitly mention this? (here? in a separate requirement?)

> A related topic is MFA fatigue attack / MFA bombing / MFA spamming. Would it be useful to explicitly mention this? (here? in a separate requirement?)
> 
How would you even defend against this other than user awareness and rate limiting? Isn’t this just the nature of the beast?

> How would you even defend against this other than user awareness and rate limiting? Isn’t this just the nature of the beast?

I think some user-interface patterns make the attack highly unlikely to be successful which makes the attack not worth it.

> I propose some small changes:
> 
> > Verify that if cross-device flows are used for authentication or delegating authorization, mitigations are in place to limit the risk of cross-device fishing. This may for example includes unique binding code or proximity checks (geolocation, network, NFC, BLE, etc).
> 
> Changes:
> 
>     * cross-device solutions → cross-device flows
> 
>     * device code phising → cross-device fishing
> 
>     * unique QR codes → unique binding code
> 
>     * move the proximity checks at the end (because I feel they are less widely applicable)
> 
>     * add NFC and BLE as a proximity check

This looks good to me, maybe a small change to make "unique binding code" more concrete we could have QR code as an example since it is a common way to do this.

> Verify that if cross-device flows are used for authentication or delegating authorization, mitigations are in place to limit the risk of cross-device fishing. This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes) or proximity checks (geolocation, network, NFC, BLE, etc).

@randomstuff I suggest open a new issue for "MFA spamming" where we can continue with the discussion for a separate requirement, so this is focused on "cross-device flows", even if it is related...

> @randomstuff I suggest open a new issue for "MFA spamming" where we can continue with the discussion for a separate requirement, so this is focused on "cross-device flows", even if it is related...

We have 
> V2.7.8 Verify that, where push notifications are used for multi-factor authentication, rate limiting or number matching is used to prevent push bombing attacks.
<del>Yes, that should be enough sorry.</del> → This comment is supposed to go to #2755
I still think a new requirement that somehow addresses _Device code flow phishing_ would be prudent.

I'm not familiar with cross-device flow and when I'm reading the proposed requirement, I can not understand what it requires me to do or is it in the application responsibility area?

> proximity checks (geolocation, network, NFC, BLE, etc).

Be sure it is not covered by:
> 4.1.8 [ADDED] Verify that adaptive security controls related to authentication and authorization decisions based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (such as time of day, location, IP address, or device) are implemented as defined in access control documentation.

Yes, I think this is also partly covered by 2.7.3 (unique binding code) and  4.1.8 overlaps the "proximity checks" part,  but "device flow authorization" does not fit so good in the authentication chapter, and a requirement for that is good to have. It as an OAuth RFC, so maybe this should be in the OAuth chapter after all?

Then it could be like this (in the Authorization Server section)

> Verify that if cross-device flows are used (i. e. OAuth Device Authorization Grant), mitigations are in place to limit the risk of cross-device phishing. This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes) or proximity checks (geolocation, network, NFC, BLE, etc).

And add https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security to the list of RFCs.
What is the application's responsibility in this scenario?

The OAuth AS needs to provide "unique binding code", verify code and additional "proximity checks" to assert that the consumption device and the authorization device are close to each other.

The client (devices) only need to implement the flow accordingly, so I think the suggested requirement is for the AS (if added, maybe level 2)?

(((🤔 FWIW, I feel that proximity information is quite unreliable in most scenarios and I have doubts on the facts that mentioning (/recommending) "proximity checks" as part of this requirement is so great.)))

Proximity is one of 17 mitigations in the RFC...I think we have two questions:
- Should we have this kind of verification in the 51.4 section or 2.7? Or not at all?
- Which of the mitigations should we have as examples?

Maybe just have this?

> Verify that if cross-device flows are used (i. e. OAuth Device Authorization Grant), mitigations are in place to limit the risk of cross-device phishing. This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes).

As I said (https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2618#issuecomment-2745128882), I'm not familiar with this flow, but I think the question is not answered:
> What is the application's responsibility in this scenario?

So this is communication between external device and the AS? How the application is related with all that? What is responsibility for the application?

> This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes).

What exactly it means? Who need to what with that?

> > This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes).
>
> What exactly it means? Who need to what with that?

We should be flexible in this regard. There are several (at least two) viable solutions for this (which are implemented in different protocols):

* When using **OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant**, the *AS* generates a unique code which is sent to the client, from there to the user, from there in the AS again (and the code can be embedded in a URL which can be transmitted to the user for example as a QR code).
* When using the **User Code Interaction of GNAP**, it works basically the same way AFAIU.
* When using **CIBA**, the *client* generates a binding message (code) which,
  1. is sent directly to the user (eg. through the client UI)
  2. is sent as well to the AS, from there to the user, and from there displayed to the user (eg. through push notification);
  3. the user is then expected to check that the two values match.

However much I try, I can not justify this as a requirement in ASVS, maybe I still lack some knowledge in the field or on the precise flow.

The requirement must be clear, testable and in scope of ASVS. Mitigate phishing attacks by going immediately to the gray area of being clear and testable. If the actual defense relies on external devices, the scope question is valid. The secret generation and handling on the application side should be handled by other and more general requirements.

If someone is really-really sure that we need to have this as a separate requirement and is willing to explain to me the aspects that need to be satisfied to have a requirement in the ASVS, I'm happy to get a requirement in. So far, I can not see that it is a match for ASVS.

ping @randomstuff @jmanico @TobiasAhnoff

> Mitigate phishing attacks by going immediately to the gray area of being clear and testable.

Yes, I agree with that. That's what I was trying to say about the "proximity checks".

Having a requirement about having a "binding code" to bind the consumption-device session and the authentication-device session, might still makes sense if this is not covered somewhere else. However, it may not be critical if we don't have it. One problem is that this "binding code" is probably one technical solution among others: it may not make sense to require its usage. This leaves us to using a vague wording such as the ones we propose which is not so great.

So I'm OK if we drop this requirement for now. I'm OK as well if we proceed with something based on the latest proposed wording.
I think this is a reasonable argument @elarlang and unless someone else has a strong charge on this I am happy to close it out. This is mostly about TV's and similar devices, not web apps.

So I'll close this now. It can be always re-opened if there are reasons to discuss it again.

Interesting topic, but can not build a clear requirement out of that.
